title: IPv4 Addressing Basics
summary: An IPv4 address is four numbers (0-255) separated by dots - every device on a network needs one to be reached.
quick_actions: An IPv4 address (e.g. 192.168.1.42) is four 8-bit numbers (0-255 each, called octets) separated by dots.
A subnet mask (e.g. 255.255.255.0) or CIDR prefix (e.g. /24) marks which part of the address is the network and which part is the specific device (host) - see the CIDR/subnet reference below.
Two devices can only talk directly, without a router in between, if they're on the same subnet.
IPv6 addresses are longer (128-bit, written in hex groups like 2001:0db8::1) - they exist because the pool of possible IPv4 addresses ran out.
more_info: This PirateBox's own visitor Wi-Fi network hands out addresses in a private range (see Private IP Ranges below) via its own DHCP server - the same mechanism any home router uses.

title: Private IP Address Ranges & Loopback
summary: Certain address ranges are reserved for private networks and never routed on the public internet.
quick_actions: 192.168.0.0/16 is the range most home routers and access points (including this one) use.
10.0.0.0/8 and 172.16.0.0/12 are the other two private ranges - more common on larger/enterprise networks.

169.254.0.0/16 (link-local/APIPA) is auto-assigned when a device expects DHCP but gets no response - seeing an address in this range usually means something's misconfigured, not that networking is working normally.
127.0.0.0/8 (loopback, 'localhost') always refers to the device itself and never touches physical network hardware.

table.name: Link-local (APIPA)
table.typical_use: Auto-assigned when DHCP fails - a sign of a problem

more_info: These ranges are permanently reserved by IETF standard and never appear as a real address on the public internet - seeing one in your own device's network settings is normal, not a sign of a misconfigured public-facing address.

title: CIDR Prefix <-> Subnet Mask Reference
summary: A /24 and a 255.255.255.0 subnet mask are two ways of writing the exact same thing.
quick_actions: The CIDR number after the slash (e.g. /24) is how many bits, counting from the left, belong to the network portion of the address.
A smaller number after the slash means a BIGGER network (more possible host addresses); a bigger number means a SMALLER network - this trips people up constantly.
Usable host addresses = 2^(32 minus the prefix) minus 2 (one address is reserved for the network itself, one for the broadcast address).
table_caption: Common CIDR prefixes and their subnet masks
more_info: /31 and /32 are deliberately left off this table - they're special cases (point-to-point links and single-host routes) that don't follow the same 'usable hosts' arithmetic as the ranges above, and including a wrong-looking number for them would be more confusing than helpful.

title: DNS & DHCP: What They Actually Do
summary: DNS translates names to addresses; DHCP hands out addresses automatically - two different jobs, often confused.
quick_actions: DNS (Domain Name System) translates a domain name (example.com) into an IP address - it's a lookup service, nothing more.
DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) automatically hands a joining device an IP address, subnet mask, gateway, and DNS server - without it, every device would need those typed in manually.
This PirateBox's own dnsmasq process serves both roles at once for its visitor Wi-Fi network - a single lightweight program providing both DNS and DHCP is common on small routers/APs.
If DNS is down but you already know a server's raw IP address, you can often still reach it directly - a DNS failure doesn't necessarily mean the underlying network is down.

title: Common Ports & Protocols
summary: A port number identifies which specific service on a device a connection is meant for.
quick_actions: An IP address gets a connection to the right device; a port number gets it to the right program/service on that device.
Ports 0-1023 are 'well-known' ports traditionally reserved for standard services - the ones below are the most likely to matter day-to-day.

more_info: Telnet (port 23) is deliberately left off as a 'use this' entry - it sends everything, including passwords, unencrypted, and has been superseded by SSH for essentially every use case.

title: Wi-Fi Terminology
summary: SSID, band, and security-standard terms explained plainly.
quick_actions: SSID is the network's name, exactly as it shows up in a device's Wi-Fi list.
2.4 GHz travels farther and penetrates walls better but is slower and more congested; 5 GHz is faster with less interference but has shorter range.
WPA2 and WPA3 are the current security/encryption standards - WEP and the original WPA are obsolete and insecure; avoid them if a device still offers them.
Signal strength is commonly shown in dBm - see Radio Reference's Decibels (dB/dBm) guide for what that number actually means. Roughly: -50 dBm is strong, -80 dBm or weaker is marginal.

title: Ethernet & Cabling Basics
summary: RJ45 connectors, cable categories, and why 'crossover cable' advice is mostly obsolete now.
quick_actions: RJ45 is the standard 8-pin connector used on virtually all Ethernet cables.
Cat5e supports up to 1 Gbps; Cat6 supports up to 10 Gbps over shorter runs - the category is usually printed right on the cable jacket.

Modern network ports auto-negotiate speed/duplex and auto-correct straight-through vs. crossover wiring (Auto-MDI-X) - needing a special 'crossover cable' is largely obsolete on hardware from the last 15+ years.
A solid link light confirms a physical connection exists - it does not by itself confirm the network or internet is actually working beyond that cable.

title: USB & Serial Basics
summary: USB-C is a connector shape, not a speed - and serial devices need both ends to agree on a baud rate.
quick_actions: USB 2.0 tops out around 480 Mbps; USB 3.x ranges 5-20 Gbps depending on generation; USB4 reaches up to 40 Gbps - the connector shape (including USB-C) doesn't by itself guarantee any particular speed.
Serial (RS-232/UART) connections use a 'baud rate' (e.g. 9600, 115200) - both ends must agree on the same rate or the data reads as garbage characters.
9600 and 115200 are the two baud rates most likely to work if you don't already know a specific device's rate.
A USB-to-serial adapter is the common way to get a serial console port on a modern computer, since most no longer have a built-in one.

title: Checksums & Hashes: Verifying File Integrity
summary: A hash is a fixed-length fingerprint of a file's contents - useful for catching corruption or tampering.
quick_actions: A checksum/hash is a short, fixed-length fingerprint calculated from a file's contents - change even one bit of the file and the fingerprint changes completely.
Comparing a downloaded file's hash to the one published by its source confirms the download wasn't corrupted or altered in transit - it does NOT by itself prove the source is trustworthy.

MD5 and SHA-1 are fast but no longer considered secure against deliberate tampering (practical collisions exist) - still fine for catching accidental corruption, not for security-critical verification.
SHA-256 (part of the SHA-2 family) is the current common standard where security actually matters.

title: Text Encoding: ASCII, UTF-8 & Unicode
summary: Garbled text on screen is usually a wrong encoding guess, not corrupted data.
quick_actions: ASCII covers only 128 characters (basic English letters/digits/punctuation) - it cannot represent accented letters, most non-English scripts, or emoji.
Unicode is a standard that assigns a unique number to essentially every character in every writing system in current or historical use.

UTF-8 is the dominant way to actually store/transmit Unicode text as bytes - it's backward-compatible with plain ASCII (every valid ASCII file is already valid UTF-8), a major reason for its near-universal adoption.
Garbled/mismatched symbols on screen ('mojibake') usually mean the text is being read with the wrong encoding assumption, not that the underlying data is actually corrupted.
